newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Proton long-term future seen intact.
newsitem.headline: Proton long-term future seen intact.

text.p: The death of Yahaya Ahmad, chairman of Malaysia's national car maker Proton, shocked local businessmen and markets on Tuesday, but analysts and government officials were confident about the firm's long-term future.
Yahaya and his wife Rohana Othman were among three people killed in a helicopter crash late on Monday night near Kuala Lipis in eastern Malaysia. The cause of the crash has not been determined.
The wealthy Yahaya also controlled the DRB-Hicom group of companies and had key holdings in the transportation industry.

"For the six to 12-month period, nothing has changed fundamentally. The policy and management teams are in place," said Chung Yee Wah, automotive analyst at equities research house HSBC James Capel in Kuala Lumpur.

Shares of Proton, car distributor Edaran Otomobil Nasional Bhd, vehicle assembler Diversified Resources Bhd, Kedah Cement Holdings Bhd and heavy industrial firm Hicom Holdings Bhd remained on his 'buy' list, Chung said.
Shares of those companies and those of Gadek (Malaysia) Bhd and Gadek Capital Bhd were suspended at the companies' request following Yahaya's death.
"In the immediate term, it will be a shock to the market, but fortunately all the stocks have been suspended," Chung said.

Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim bolstered the view that Proton's future was assured, saying, "...we will be committed to continue to support all the projects undertaken within the group," the Bernama news agency reported.
Proton has a market capitalisation of 8.67 billion ringgit ($3.5 billion).
Yahaya was lauded for the 51 million sterling ($83 million) acquisition of ailing British sports car maker Lotus in 1996. Analysts said the Lotus deal would transfer much-needed technology.
"The deal with Lotus is probably not in any jeopardy, as it has been signed and sealed," said a senior analyst at a foreign research house in Kuala Lumpur.

Prime Minister Mahathir handed Yahaya the chairmanship of Proton in 1995. With Malaysia's car market facing deregulation towards 1999, Yahaya was charged with revamping the company to equip it for the onslaught of international competition.
For the year ended March 31, 1996, Proton reported a net profit of 356 million ringgit versus 232 million a year ago.

"His death should not affect the existing business of the group, but future business may suffer a bit. Yahaya's plans for the group will be put on hold," said Choo Swee Kee, automotive analyst at research house Vickers Ballas.
"(Proton deputy chairman) Salleh Sulong will take over the running of Proton until the government decides who will succeed Yahaya," he added.
Officials at Proton were not immediately available for comment. But sources at the company said they expected some jockeying for senior positions after Yahaya's death.
The sources said there were "two visible camps" in the company now, one created by Yahaya and one by former managing director Nadzmi Mohamed Salleh, who quit Proton last year.
"Those trained by Nadzmi have never really been comfortable working with Yahaya's team," a source at Proton told Reuters.
